tips.title: The 3-question article test
tips.body: Before any noun, ask: (1) Is it countable? (2) Is it specific/identified? (3) Am I referring to it in general? Uncountable + general = zero article. Countable + first mention = a/an. Identified/specific = the.

tips.title: Beware of 'the + abstract noun'
tips.body: In IELTS essays, writers overuse 'the' before abstract concepts: ✗ 'The education is important' → ✓ 'Education is important'. Only use 'the' if you mean a specific instance: 'The education system in Vietnam needs reform.'

tips.title: Second-mention rule in Task 1
tips.body: In graph descriptions, introduce a data point with 'a' (or no article for uncountable), then switch to 'the' on the next reference. Example: 'There was a sharp rise in 2010. The rise was followed by a plateau.' This signals you're tracking the same data point.

tips.title: Task 1: anchor your tense to the graph's time frame
tips.body: Check whether the data is historical, current, or projected. Historical (2000–2020) → simple past. Current trend (ongoing) → present perfect or present. Future projection (2030, 'is forecast to') → will / is expected to. Mix tenses only when the graph itself spans multiple time zones.

tips.title: Task 2: use present simple for your argument, past only for evidence
tips.body: Your main claims and opinions use present simple: 'Globalisation increases inequality.' Only switch to past when citing historical evidence: 'The 2008 financial crisis showed that…'. A paragraph that shifts between past and present without reason signals poor tense control to examiners.

tips.title: Perfect aspect vs simple past: it depends on relevance now
tips.body: Use present perfect ('has increased') when the past event still has present relevance. Use simple past ('increased') when it's complete with no current connection. In Task 2 body paragraphs, simple past is usually safer — perfect is for introductions and overviews.

tips.title: Identify the true subject, not the nearest noun
tips.body: Long noun phrases bury the real subject: 'The number of people who live in urban areas [is/are]?' — the subject is 'number', so it's 'is'. Strip out the prepositional phrase and relative clause to find the head noun, then match the verb.

tips.title: 'The number of' vs 'a number of' — they take opposite verbs
tips.body: 'The number of + plural noun' = singular verb: 'The number of accidents is rising.' 'A number of + plural noun' = plural verb: 'A number of accidents have been reported.' Memorise this pair — it appears in almost every IELTS mock test.

tips.title: Collective nouns in academic writing: default to singular
tips.body: In academic IELTS writing, treat collective nouns as singular: the government HAS, the team IS, the committee HAS DECIDED. British English allows plural (the government ARE), but singular is safer for IELTS and avoids mixed-number errors within the same paragraph.

tips.title: Learn prepositions by chunk, not by rule
tips.body: English prepositions follow convention more than logic. Build a personal list of 20 high-frequency academic chunks: 'responsible FOR', 'result IN', 'contribute TO', 'depend ON', 'associated WITH'. Read them aloud until they sound right — ear memory beats rule memory for prepositions.

tips.title: Watch for verb-to-preposition chains
tips.body: When you nominalise a verb (turn it into a noun), its preposition sometimes changes: 'invest IN' (verb) → 'investment IN' (noun). But 'contribute TO' → 'contribution TO'. Check each noun-preposition pair separately; don't assume the verb's preposition transfers.

tips.title: Spot-check your prepositions in the final minute
tips.body: In the last 60 seconds of IELTS Writing, scan your essay for the five highest-error prepositions in academic texts: in/on/at (time + place), for/of (relationship), with/by (agent/manner). Don't reread for content — just hunt these words specifically.

tips.title: Map the four forms for your key vocabulary
tips.body: For every important word you plan to use in an essay, know all four forms before the exam: noun / verb / adjective / adverb. Example: pollution / pollute / polluted, polluting / — . Write a 10-word vocabulary table for each topic you prepare (environment, technology, health).

tips.title: Suffix signals the word class
tips.body: Use suffixes as a quick check: -tion/-sion/-ment/-ance = noun; -ify/-ise/-ate = verb; -ive/-al/-ic/-ous = adjective; -ly = adverb (usually). If your sentence needs a verb but you've written a -tion word, flag it for correction.

tips.title: Avoid stacking nouns — convert to adjective + noun
tips.body: A very common word-form error in IELTS essays: 'the economy development' (two nouns stacked). Convert to 'economic development' (adjective + noun). Scan your essay for any sequence of [noun] + [noun] — one of them likely needs to be in adjective form.

tips.title: One connector per clause boundary
tips.body: The most common sentence structure error in IELTS is the 'although…, but…' double connector. A clause can only have one subordinator or coordinator at its junction. Write it, then check: is there exactly one connector linking these two ideas? If you see two, delete one.

tips.title: Vary sentence length intentionally, not by accident
tips.body: IELTS Band 7+ requires sentence variety. After writing a paragraph, check: are all sentences roughly the same length? If yes, deliberately break one long sentence into two shorter ones, or combine two short ones with a conjunction. Aim for a mix of 10–15 word and 20–30 word sentences.

tips.title: Fronted adverbials are your safest complexity move
tips.body: Adding a subordinate clause at the front of a sentence is the simplest way to demonstrate complex sentence structure without risk. 'Although this view has merit, it overlooks…' / 'While governments play a role, individuals must also…'. These are formulaic but always grammatically safe.

tips.title: Conjunctive adverbs always need a comma after them
tips.body: Words like However, Therefore, Furthermore, Nevertheless, In addition, As a result — when they start a sentence — must be followed by a comma. This is not optional. Examiners mark 'However the...' as a punctuation error that affects the Grammatical Range and Accuracy band.

tips.title: Semicolons and colons: one safe use each
tips.body: Semicolon: join two independent clauses that are closely related. 'Obesity is rising; governments must respond.' Colon: introduce a list or explanation. 'There are two main causes: diet and exercise.' Using either of these correctly signals higher-band control to examiners.

tips.title: Never use a comma before 'that', 'because', or 'since' (when causal)
tips.body: Subordinating conjunctions (that, because, since, when, if, although) do NOT require a comma before them when they follow the main clause: ✗ 'It is clear, that education matters' → ✓ 'It is clear that education matters'. Commas go before coordinating conjunctions (but, so, yet, for), not subordinators.

tips.title: The IELTS uncountable noun blacklist
tips.body: Memorise these 12 words that can NEVER be pluralised in IELTS essays: information, advice, research, evidence, knowledge, furniture, equipment, money, traffic, news, progress, homework. If you write 'informations' or 'advices', it is an immediate error.

tips.title: Quantifiers signal whether a noun should be singular or plural
tips.body: Count nouns (book, student, country) use: many, few, a few, several, a number of — with plural form. Uncount nouns use: much, little, a little, a great deal of, a lack of — with singular form. Getting these pairings right avoids a cluster of errors in one sentence.

tips.title: Criteria, phenomena, data — know your Latin plurals
tips.body: Academic writing frequently uses words with Latin/Greek plurals: criterion (sing.) / criteria (pl.); phenomenon / phenomena; medium / media; datum / data. In IELTS academic essays, 'data' is typically treated as plural: 'The data show…' though 'The data shows…' is increasingly accepted.

tips.title: When unsure, use a neutral verb + noun
tips.body: If you are not sure whether 'do', 'make', or 'take' collocates with a noun, use a more academic verb: instead of 'do a research', write 'conduct research / carry out research'. Instead of 'make a solution', write 'develop a solution / propose a solution'. Precise verbs also improve your lexical score.

tips.title: Strong/heavy/high/large — learn which adjective goes with which noun
tips.body: These four adjectives are often confused: STRONG (argument, evidence, link, influence), HEAVY (rain, traffic, smoker, burden), HIGH (rate, level, demand, temperature), LARGE (number, proportion, scale, amount). When you use an intensifying adjective, pause and ask: have I seen this exact phrase in academic text?

tips.title: Read collocations in context, not in isolation
tips.body: The best way to expand collocation accuracy for IELTS is to read the Cambridge English Corpus example sentences, not just dictionary definitions. For every new academic word you learn, find 2 collocations: the noun it commonly precedes, and the verb it commonly follows.

tips.title: Government, society, committee = 'it', not 'they'
tips.body: In IELTS academic writing, singular collective nouns take singular pronouns: 'The government must increase its budget' (not 'their budget'). 'Society should reconsider its values.' Using 'they' for these nouns is accepted in informal English but marked as an error in IELTS academic writing.

tips.title: Repeat the noun rather than use an unclear pronoun
tips.body: When 'it' or 'they' could refer to more than one noun in the previous sentence, simply repeat the noun: ✗ 'The policy affected the economy. It was significant.' → ✓ 'The policy affected the economy. The impact was significant.' Clarity > elegance in IELTS.

tips.title: Avoid first-person and second-person pronouns in Task 2
tips.body: IELTS Task 2 is academic writing. Avoid 'you', 'we' (referring to the reader), and overuse of 'I'. 'I think' once in an opinion essay is acceptable; 'I believe, in my opinion, I feel, I personally think' in the same essay signals a lack of formal register. Use 'It is argued that…' or 'This suggests…' instead.

tips.title: The subject of the main clause must be the doer of the participle
tips.body: When a sentence starts with a participial phrase (Being…, Having studied…, Considering…), the very next noun after the comma must be the person/thing doing the action. ✗ 'Being a student, the exam was difficult.' → Who is a student? The exam? ✓ 'Being a student, I found the exam difficult.'

tips.title: Move adverbs close to the word they modify
tips.body: Misplaced adverbs create ambiguity: 'Only governments can solve the problem' (governments alone can solve it) vs 'Governments can only solve the problem' (the only thing they can do is solve it). In IELTS essays, place 'only', 'even', 'just', 'almost', 'nearly' directly before the word they qualify.

tips.title: One comparative marker per comparison
tips.body: Never write 'more + -er' (more higher, more better) or 'most + -est' (most fastest). Short adjectives (1–2 syllables): add -er/-est. Long adjectives (3+ syllables): use more/most. Irregular: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, far/further/furthest.

tips.title: Compare like with like using 'that of' / 'those of'
tips.body: A very common IELTS Task 1 error: 'The rate in China was higher than Japan.' You are comparing a rate with a country. Fix: 'The rate in China was higher than that in Japan.' / 'The rates in China were higher than those in Japan.' This is a quick Band 7 accuracy fix.

tips.title: Use 'as…as' for equality comparisons, 'not as…as' for negative
tips.body: 'As fast as' = equal speed. 'Not as fast as' = slower. Never mix: ✗ 'as fast than', ✗ 'more fast as'. For IELTS Task 1, the structure 'X was roughly the same as Y' or 'X was comparable to Y' is a safer alternative when exact equality is shown in the graph.
